notes: Every report is run on its own so its result is attributable.

A passing report is not sufficient on its own, and a resource campaign has a failure mode the other campaigns do not: a bound can be reported as holding by a run that never approached it. A worker budget of 64 whose observed peak was 3, a page bound checked against four rows, and a queue that was never filled are all green and none is evidence about a ceiling. So each report retains an observation into a directory this runner creates empty, and the runner requires every declared resource to have been observed, every live ceiling to have been reached exactly, and every shedding resource to have been offered an overload and to have shed.
The stressed run is required to have left the same durable record as the sequential baseline, because a concurrency result that changes a durable observation is invalid regardless of its throughput.

Each database report is required to name the PostgreSQL major it ran against, because a matrix point is invisible in a connection string and an observation from one supported major would otherwise reconcile perfectly inside a run of another.

The denominator this reconciles against is checked from the other side by an ordinary cargo test, which parses every library crate and fails when a constant declared under the repository's bound declaration convention is neither proved nor argued out of scope. That convention is what the guarantee is bounded by: a ceiling written as a bare literal or named outside it is ruled out by review rather than by the scan.

out_of_scope.reason: A timeout bounds how long one operation may take, not how much of a resource is concurrently held, and the capacity budget declares none of these. They are validated at construction like every other bound here, and their validation is covered by the configuration tests that own them.

The retry attempt ceiling and the backoff ceiling bound a policy a definition declares, not a resource the framework holds. The retry cache those attempts write into is in scope, and is the resource the performance plan names.

These bound when a decision may be taken, not how much may be held. A stale-execution threshold that is wrong produces a premature or delayed recovery decision, which is a lifecycle result rather than a resource result.

The bound exists, but the campaign cannot construct past it: it is checked inside CursorKey::encode, a private method on a #[non_exhaustive] enum whose Name variant cannot be constructed outside crates/oxide-batch-repository itself. bounded-identifier-text's other twelve subjects are all reachable through a public constructor this campaign calls directly; this one is not, and the campaign records that honestly rather than adding a thirteenth subject no evidence would ever exercise.

The bound is a raw byte cutoff on an interactive io::stdin() read inside a private, non-exported read_confirmation function, not a validated identifier or reference type constructed from a caller-supplied string like bounded-identifier-text's other subjects. It is unreachable from this campaign's non-interactive harness, and no existing test in this repository exercises its limit either.

Explicitly outside the M0-M4 framework boundary. The capacity budget already states that application readers, writers, and item buffers are budgeted by the workload, and the framework declares no ceiling for them, so the campaign has nothing to prove and does not pretend to.

out_of_scope.reason: These are framework-declared ceilings, but on the byte length of a caller-supplied constructor input string (a resource identity or object key), not on a resource the M0-M4 capacity budget names or the campaign's runtime resource-bound model covers. `MAX_RESOURCE_IDENTITY_BYTES` (`item_components::multi_resource::ResourceIdentity`) and `MAX_OBJECT_KEY_BYTES` (`item_components::object_store::ObjectIdentity`), added in #150, sit in the same category as every other `XxxTooLong` constructor validation in this crate (e.g. `StateSchemaId`'s byte bound): a fixed-string-length input check enforced once at construction, not a bounded operational resource (queue, buffer, connection, cache) whose steady-state behavior this campaign proves.
No remote worker, broker credit, or assignment queue exists in the accepted M0-M4 scope. A campaign row for one would be a claim about unwritten code.

ChunkTimeThreshold bounds how long a TimeCompletionPolicy or AdaptiveCompletionPolicy waits before deciding a chunk is complete, not how much of a resource is concurrently held -- the same category as the operation-timeouts entry above, just for a completion decision rather than a database operation. The enclosing ChunkSize ceiling remains the actual buffering resource bound while the threshold has not elapsed. Added in #151/#179.

These bound the shape of a CompositeCompletionPolicy tree an application constructs -- member count and nesting depth -- not a resource the framework holds at runtime. Both are validated once at CompositeCompletionPolicy::new, in the same category as MAX_RESOURCE_IDENTITY_BYTES/MAX_OBJECT_KEY_BYTES above: a fixed structural check enforced at construction, not a bounded operational resource (queue, buffer, connection, cache) whose steady-state behavior this campaign proves. Added in #151/#179.

informational_symbols.reason: StateLimits::default()'s byte limit (65536), a genuinely different number from MAXIMUM_BYTES (1048576), not an alias of it. It is the config value a definition gets when it chooses none of its own, not itself a ceiling: nothing refuses a value one byte past it, since a definition remains free to configure any limit up to MAXIMUM_BYTES. There is no boundary to construct.

StateLimits::default()'s depth limit (16), independently different from MAXIMUM_DEPTH (64) for the same reason DEFAULT_MAXIMUM_BYTES is: a default config value inside the allowed range, not an enforced ceiling with a refusal past it.

An internal VecDeque::with_capacity hint and the total-events default, not an independent ceiling: IncidentEventBuffer::new validates total >= per_execution, never an absolute maximum on total, so there is no value one past which construction is refused. MAX_RETAINED_EVENTS_PER_EXECUTION is the real, independently enforced ceiling and is already proven both sides.

stress.note: A ceiling is only proved by a run that reached it. A worker budget of 64 whose observed peak was 3 is evidence about a workload, not about a bound, so each report records the load it offered and the peak it observed and the runner requires the two to be in the relation the resource's policy implies. For offered-exceeds-ceiling specifically, the runner also requires the discarded count to equal offered minus retained under the resource's own declared shedding_rule: an accounting that leaves a gap unattributed is not shedding, it is loss the report failed to count.

requirements.detail: The offered partition count is several times the worker budget, so the ceiling is reachable, and the observed peak must equal it. A peak below the ceiling means the run never filled the worker set and proves nothing about the bound; a peak above it is the failure the report exists to catch.

The split declares more branches than the branch budget admits, so the ceiling is reachable and the observed peak must equal it. This is the budgeted run's own proof; the declared ceiling's own reachability is proved separately by the dual-budget-boundary check against this resource's ceiling_run detail.
The short-pool attempt must be refused before a job execution exists, so the rejection is observable as an absence in the database rather than only as an error value.
The database holds several times a full page, so a page that returned everything would exceed the bound rather than satisfy it.
The purge is planned against more candidates than the batch bound admits, so a plan that took them all would exceed the bound.
More records are offered than the queue holds, so the drop path is entered rather than described. The drop count must be the excess exactly, and batch work must complete while the queue is saturated.
More label combinations are offered than the family budget admits, so the reserved series is reached rather than assumed.
More events are emitted for one execution than the buffer retains, so the eviction rule is exercised.

The rendered response is offered at several times the operator output bound, in the same bytes the bound is stated in, so the truncation path is entered and the discarded count is the excess exactly, the same accounting every other offered-exceeds-ceiling resource owes.
